ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Simplification of extradition laws 
*41.  SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA:†† 
SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the efforts Government have made with other countries to simplify 
extradition laws; and 
(b) the progress made in this regard, so for? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) Extradition treaties are 
negotiated to facilitate and enable extradition of fugitives. Each treaty has to 
be discussed taking into account the legal system of India and the contracting 
parties. 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, at the outset, I would like 
to congratulate the Minister for getting Dawood's brother repatriated to India, 
yesterday. But, at the same time, I would like to know from him why are the 
diplomatic efforts not being made to have extradition treaties with more and more 
countries? At present, out of 143 countires, we have extradition treaties with 
only 13 countries. I would like to know from the Minister whether any efforts 
are being made to have such kind of treaties with other countries also. 
SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH: Sir, it is the policy of the Government of 
India to conclude extradition treaties with as many countries as possible. 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Rajeev Shukla. 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
Proposals are initiated after ascertaining the interests of other countries in 
concluding the extradition treaties with India. As far as treaties are concerned, 
we have already concluded extradition treaties with 19 countries. We have 
come to a point where treaties will be concluded with seven countries; and we 
have initiated a proposal for having extradition treaties with 30 countries. 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Is it not a fact that the pace is very slow? My 
second supplementary is—the way international terrorism is growing, why has 
India not signed the UN Convention onTrans-National Organised Crime as yet? 
SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH: That proposal is under consideration of the 
Government of India and we will be doing it very soon.

*45. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of DISINVESTMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that overall performance of the National 
Fertilizers Limited (NFL) is very impressive and its net profit after tax 
deduction during the last fiscal year has been registered at Rs. 40.61 crores 
against Rs. 27.31 crores in 2000-2001 ;

decision to divest 51 per cent of its equity;

disinvestment of NFL; and

THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a,    
^d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Disinvestment in Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs) is 
being undertaken as per the declared policy of the Government to bring down its 
equity in non-strategic CPSUs to 26% or below in generality of cases. The non-
strategic CPSUs are those, which are not in the areas of arms & ammunitions 
and allied items of defence equipment, defence aircrafts and warships, atomic 
energy (except in the areas related to the generation of nucl.ar power and 
applications of radiations and radio- 
8 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
isotopes to agriculture, medicine an d non-strategic industries) and railway 
transport.This policy is applicable to profit-making as well as loss-making 
CPSUs. In accordance with the recommendations of the Disinvestment 
Commission, the Government has decided to disinvest its equity in National 
Fertilisers Limited as it operates in the non-strategic sector. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise in view of reply to (c) above.

Statement 
(a) to (e) Government had strongly protested against the harassment of 
Indian Charge d'Affaires by Pakistani Intelligence offiicials on 18th January, 
2003. Indian officials in the High Commission in Islamabad, including 
Charge d'Affaires, are routinely subjected to threatening telephone calls, 
intimidatory and obstructive surveillance and offensive behaviour. 
Pakistan expelled four Indian officials on January 23,2003 and five 
more officials including the Charge d'Affaires on February 8, 2003. 
Pakistan's actions were a clear and unjustified retaliation, based on an 
approach of compulsive hostility, to the necessary measures Government had 
taken in view of the involvement of officials of Pakistan High Commission, 
including their Cd'A, in funding of terrorist and secessionist activities 
directed against India, and in activities incompatible with their official status. 
Under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961 and the 
bilateral "Code of Conduct for Treatment of Diplomatic/Consular Personnel 
in India and Pakistan" signed by the two countries in 1992, the responsibility 
for the safety and security of personnel of High Commission rests with the 
host Government. Government of India protests strongly to Government of 
Pakistan against all cases of harassment of officials of Indian High 
Commission in Islamabad and reminds them of their obligations under the 
Vienna Convention and bilateral Code of Conduct. Government remains 
committed to taking all necessary measures for the safety and security of the 
personnel in Indian Missions abroad.

Statement-1 
 IT. Schemes for rural areas 
1. The Department of Information Technology, Ministry of 
Communications & Information Technology has undertaken a scheme for 
setting up Community Information Centres (CICs) at 487 block 
headquarters in the seven North-East states and Sikkim for promoting 
application of Information Technology for accelerating socio-economic 
development of the region.The scheme is being implemented in the states 
of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, 
Tripura and Sikkim. 475 CICs have been setup till date. 
The project is mainly aimed at bridging the digital divide and providing 
connectivity at the grass root level particularly in those areas where the benefits 
of national development have not reached the community, specially women and 
children to the desired extent as they have all along been deprived of access to 
information relevant to their needs. 
2. E-lnfrastructure and E-Learning Group has no comprehensive 
scheme for rural and tribal areas. However, pilot implementation of Rural IT 
Centres (Samadhan Kendras) has been completed in Ramanathapuram Distt. of 
Tamil Nadu and 3 more Samadhan Kendra projects were launched in Ujjain (MP), 
West godavari Distt. (AP), and Chitrakoot (MP). Out of these Samadhan 
Kendra projects at Chitrakoot (MP) and Ujjain (MP), have been completed. 
These provide connectivity to internet as well as email and computer facilities 
to the villagers through localised centres. Besides this, a whole range of other 
information facilities required in rural areas are fulfilled through Samadhan 
Kendras. 
3. A Centrally Sponsored Scheme on computerisation of Land Records 
(CLR) is being implemented in the country since 1988-89 which included rural 
and tribal areas also. This Scheme is being implemented jointly by Minister of 
Rural Development and National Informatics Centre (NIC). Funds are being 
provided by Minister of Rural Development to States/UTs for installations of 
Computers at District and TehsilsAaluk centres and so far 582 districts and 
2959 tehsils/taluks/blocks of the country have been brought under the 
programme. 
4. Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission, under the Ministry of 
Rural Development provides assistance at the rate of 100 per cent to 
75 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
the States and Union Territories for procurement of hardware, office 
automation packages, training of manpower and development of application 
software for computerisation up to the division level officers of the line 
departments. 
5. The Ministry undertook a pilot project for providing VSAT 
connectivity to 15 District Rural Development Agencies (DRDAs) for 
providing internet facilities and a web based software for poverty alleviation and 
rural development programmes. The pilot project has been taken up in 15 
districts in 11 States, namely Anantpur and Nalgonda in Andhra Pradesh, 
Thanjavur and Perambalur in Tamil Nadu, Etawah in Uttar Pradesh, Hosangabad, 
Narisinghpur and Jaisen in Madhya Pradesh, Solan in Himachal Pradesh, 
Hazaribagh in Jharkhand, Midnapur in West Bengal, Shillong in Meghalaya, 
Chandrapur in Maharashtra, SJkar in Rajasthan and Almora in Uttaranchal. The 
project endeavors to establish a system for flow of information in respect of 
Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), Jawahar Grarri Samridhi Yojana 
(JGSY), Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), Indra Awaas Yojana (IAY) and 
Watershed programmes. 
6. Other projects being implemented by NIC jointly with concerned 
Ministers viz. Agricultural Produce Markets Networking of Mandis, Social 
Welfare Pension Computerisation. ICT applications in the Rural Development 
sector, includes: (a) CRISP: Computerised Rural Information Support Project — 
Rural Soft 2000: Processes of the data related to poverty alleviation schemes 
sponsored by MRD/SRD and implementation coordinated by DRDA. (b) Rural 
Bazar: An e-commerce solution that helps DRDA's in marketing of rural products 
of SGSY beneficiaries, (c) PriaSoft: Addresses the financial management needs and 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) such as Zilla Parishad, Block Samiti and Village 
Panchayat, and is being tested at SivaGanga, Tamil Nadu, (d) ENRICH: A 
generic solution by NIC and UNESCO for usage in Community Multimedia 
Centres (CMCs) that is a one stop access, communication & delivery 
mechanism for communities, customizable in terms of local, Indian language and 
content. 
7. In another noval scheme for developing IT application for the rural and 
poor people, Media Lab Asia has been set up by the Government as a research 
company with a network of national laboratories for research, innovation and 
development, of advanced ICT technologies for the benefit of masses. Media Lab 
Asia was launched in June 2001 jointly with 
76 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Massachusetts Institute of Technology  (MIT), USA. The objective of this 
scheme is to address trie grand challenges of poverty, literacy, education, health, 
employment, and micro-entrepreneurship through the use of information and 
communication technologies (ICT), on a large co-ordinated scale, using futuristic 
technology and both academic and non-academic input with creativity, 
sensitivity, and with a focus on affordable accessibility. 
Statement-ll 
IT benefits to Hindi and other Indian languages speaking population 
Department of IT has setup 13 Resource centres for Technology 
Development in Indian Languages in various parts of the country. These centres 
have the responsibility of developing tools and technology for application/use 
of computers in all the 18 constitutionally recognised local languages of India. 
Localisation of technology and Content Creation in Hindi and making the 
content available on computer and Internet, is being spearheaded in Hindi 
speaking states under the programme: Content Development and IT 
Localisation Network (Coil-Net). 
Both the above initiatives of the Department of IT also directly/ 
indirectly benefit the rural masses. 
The IT projects implemented for rural areas by NIC (mentioned in 
Annexure I) are also in iQcal languages, and often use icon-based interfaces etc, in 
order to minimise difficulties experienced by literates/semi-literates. 
Samadhan Kendra projects already mentioned at 1.2 caters to the needs 
of rural people, hence these have strong local language interfaces apart from 
English. The contents are presented in Tamil (in Ramanathapuram 
distt.),Telugu (in West Godavri distt. AP), and Hindi in case of Ujjain and 
Chitrakoot MP).

Continuation of terrorism by Pakistan 
262. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to State: 
(a) whether there is no sign of Pakistan moving away from terrorism 
despite presence of Indian Army on the borders for a year; and 
(b) if so, the new approach proposed for a new foreign policy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) President Musharraf committed on 
January 12, May 27 and June 6, 2002 that cross-border infiltration would be 
ended on a permanent basis, Pakistan would no longer allow its territory to be 
used for any terrorist activity anywhere in the world, and no organization in 
Pakistan would be allowed to indulge in terrorism in the name of Kashmir. 
However, cross-border infiltration aid terrorism still continue. 
Although, Pakistan took some initial action against some terrorist 
groups and arrested some low-level cadr es, there is no evidence of any firm 
action against the infrastructure in Pakistan that supports terrorism. There have 
also been reversals of some of the initial Pakistani steps including release of 
arrested terrorist leaders and cadres. Despite limited and reluctant support that 
the Pakistani establishment has provided to the international coalition against 
foreign Al-Qaeda elements, it has attempted to maintain its support and 
sponsorship of terrorist groups acting against its neighbouring countries. 
(b) The Government have been appropriately and effectively bringing to the 
attention of the international community facts pertaining to Pakistan's sponsorship 
of cross-border terrorism and are firmly resolved to take all necessary measures 
to fight against this menace. There is widespread recognition of Pakistan being 
the epicentre of international terrorism and several countries have called upon 
Pakistan to stop its sponsorship or continuing as 'platform* for international 
terrorism. 
India remains committed to resuming bilateral dialogue with Pakistan in the 
spirit of Simla Agreement and Lahore Declaration. But Pakistan must stop 
sponsorship of cross-border terrorism for dialogue to be held.

checked through enactment and enforcement of a number of labour laws aimed at 
protecting and promoting the health, safety, welfare and social security of workers. The 
Central Government has enacted a number of labour legislations to protect the workers 
from economic exploitation.These enactments are the Payment of the Wages Act, 
1936, Minimum Wages Act, 1948 and Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. The 
provisions of these enactments ensure that the workmen are paid their wages at 
regular intervals and without unauthorized deductions. These laws also ensure that 
the workers employed in the scheduled employments and in the unorganized 
sector are paid the wages which are not less than the minimum rates of wages fixed 
by the appropriate Governments. Further, the Equal Remuneration Act has been 
enacted to provide for payment of equal wages to female workers as paid to the 
male workers when employed to do same work or work of similar nature. 
These enactments also provide that the aggrieved workmen can file claim 
applications/complaints before the prescribed authority in order to get their dues 
paid/settled. These Acts also provide for penalties such as fines and imprisonments 
for violation/non-compliance of the provisions of the Acts.

(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (d) Against a projected outlay of

163

realized during the plan was Rs. 4,06,687 crore. The actual realization and the 
shortfall were thus 83.1 per cent and 16.9 per cent respectively of the outlay

the Ninth Plan period was the substantial deterioration in the Balance from Current 
Revenues caused due to a stagnant level of tax revenues coupled with substantial

Development Council. It outlines various measures for raising resources 
required for financing the outlay projected for the Tenth Plan. The steps aimed

rationalization of customs and excise taxes and extension of Value Added Tax

Plan document also suggests steps for controlling non-plan revenue 
expenditure and cost recovery through levy of user charges in order to 
improve the resource position of the Government.

from remote and inaccessible areas over land.

address both Houses of Parliament, assembled together, and inform the 
Parliament of the causes of its summons. Article 87(2) provides that the 
Parliament shall discuss the matters referred to in the President's Address, and

discussed. We may discuss intentions, as well as omissions and commissions.

THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN 
SINGH): Madam Deputy Chairperson, I thank the hon. President for the

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003]

before its touchdown on 1st February, 2003. Kalpana Chawla's exemplary 
courage and determination will continue to inspire our young people for 
generations to come. Madam, I also share the President's sense of joy that the 
people of Jammu and Kashmir in the October elections to the State Assembly, 
replied to the threat of the bullet, with the power of the ballot. I sincerely hope 
that the Central Government will fully cooperate with the Government of 
Jammu & Kashmir in sustaining the process of hope and confidence created by 
the outcome of the free and fair elections, and in meeting the legitimate 
aspirations of the people of Jammu & Kashmir for a life of dignity and self-
respect. Madam, in this context, I welcome the commitment made in para 10 
of the President's Address, which says that the Centre is fully committed to 
working closely with the newly elected Government in Jammu & Kashmir in 
its efforts to bring peace, normalcy and economic development of the State. 
The Prime Minister has announced projects and schemes worth over Rs. 6000 
crores having various aspects of development and security, with a thrust on 
the generation of new employment opportunities for the youth and relief for 
migrants affected by militancy and cross-border shelling. It is my sincere hope 
that these intentions will be translated into concrete action on the ground. 
Madam, as I listened to the President delivering his Address, I felt 
his Address could be divided into three parts. The first one relates to the 
management of the economy; the second relates to the national security 
scenario and how we are meeting the challenge to our national security; and 
the third deals with foreign policy initiatives. In dealing with all these areas, 
the Address does contain some welcome statements of intentions. But I must 
confess to you, Madam, that in my view, the Address is pretty weak when it 
comes to spelling out precise strategies and programmes needed to translate 
these intentions into hard realities. The Address does not indicate that we 
have, in the Government, a firm hand for steering our economy and polity in 
the desired direction. In particular, Madam, the Address indicates a great sense 
of complacency in the ruling astablishment in meeting the grim challenge that 
certain forces which are seeking to communalise our polity pose for the future 
of our country. 
Madam, I now deal with the President's Address in so far as it has a 
bearing on the economy. In his Address, the President has referred to the 
264 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
launching of the Tenth Five Year Plan, which has set the target of eight per 
cent annual average GDP growth, with a companion target of five crore 
additional employment and self-employment opportunities, that is, one crore 
new jobs to be created every year. That our country needs a development 
strategy with an ambitious growth and employment target is unquestionable, 
and if the Government does have such a strategy, we will fully cooperate in 
implementing that strategy. But, Madam, the President's Address does not 
inspire confidence that the policies and programmes, which will facilitate the 
realisation of these ambitious targets are truly in place. Why do I say this? 
This Government has been in office now for nearly five years. And what is its 
record? In the last five years that the BJP-led Government has been in office 
at the Centre, there has been a decline in the growth-rate of national income, 
the growth-rate of industrial production, the growth-rate of agricultural 
production, as well as the growth-rate of employment, compared with the 
preceding five years. The rate of growth of GDP in the Ninth Five Year Plan, 
which ended last year, has been no more than 5 to 5.25 per cent. In the year 
2002-2003, which happens to be the first year of the Tenth Five Year Plan, 
the projected growth rate by the CSO is no more than 4.4 per cent as against 
the Plan target of eight per cent. Our per capita agricultural output has fallen 
since 1998. Despite all the claims made in the President's Address for this 
Government's solicitude for our farmers, the harsh reality is that our per 
capita agricultural output has fallen since 1998. That happens to be the period 
over which this ruling dispensation has presided over our country's destiny. 
Savings and investment rates in our economy reached a peak in 
1995-96, which was the last year of the Congress Government. Since then, 
there has been a declining tendency. What is more worrisome, and which is 
crucial for realising the type of intentions that are contained in the President's 
Address, to which I will refer a little later, is we need a high rate of savings in 
the public sector. What is the reality? In the year 1995-96, the public sector 
savings rate was 1.7 per cent of our GDP. The public sector savings rate is, 
now, negative by 1.7 per cent. There was a deterioration of full 3.5 per cent of 
our GDP in the last five years. As a result, Madam, both the fiscal and 
revenue deficits of the Centre and the States have increased sharply in the last 
five years. These deficits are, now, back to 1990-91 level, i.e., a year before 
the reform process began. 
265 

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
The public sector expenditure on infrastructure and rural 
development, as a proportion of GDP, has declined after 1995-96, and this 
has not been compensated by a rise in private investment. The inconsistent 
policies pursued by the present Government have given rise to a high degree 
of uncertainty which has adversely affected the climate for enterprise. The 
fiscal policy pursued by the BJP Government has changed directions every 
year. Year after year, there have been reversals and changes in tax policies. 
There has been no medium term or long-run thinking when it comes to tax 
policies. Tax revenues have been overestimated year after year. 
Disinvestment policies - and I say this with all respect to my 
distinguished friend, Shri Arun Shourie, - and the regulatory regimes

consistency and clarity, and have sought to promote a type of crony 
capitalism, rather than build a dynamic and competitive economy.

speculation which we have never seen before. The primary market is, 
virtually, dead, and it is dead for the last five years. The financial institutions 
like the UTI, in which over two crores of investors have reposed faith, have 
been grossly mismanaged, bringing distress to millions of small investors, 
senior citizens, widows, orphans and pensioners. 
Madam, the communalisation of our polity and the freedom given 
by this Government to the VHP and the Bajrang Dal to spread communal 
hatred in various parts of the country has further promoted a climate not 
conducive to the growth of investment. Infrastructure investments, with the

aspects of Government's policies and programmes. It is intended only to 
highlight a few areas which should be of interest to the Members of 
Parliament, and, therefore, to the people as a whole. I thought, in the Address, 
the President had dealt mainly with the working of the economy and the 
foreign policy of the country, and had not adequately dealt with a very 
important segment of our ambitions, aspirations, dreams, and, I would refer to 
the social sector. There is every reason to be proud of the achievements in the 
economy taking into account what happens in the world, as a whole, in the last 
one year, the slow-down of the economy all over the world, the great drought 
that we experienced in 14 States of the country and the shortfall in agricultural 
production. In this background, the achievements of the Government, of 
course, deserves praise and approbation; and that is what the President had 
done. But, I am of the view that adequate importance should have been given, 
if not equal, at least adequate importance should have been given to the social 
sector, particularly, to education and health care. Mr. Vce-Chairman, Sir, if I 
am asked to make an appraisal of our achievements during the 52 or 53 years 
of our Republic and present in a very short form where we went wrong most, I 
will put my finger on the 
292 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
social sector. We have immense achievements to our credit in the last half a 
century of our existence as a Republic. In science and technology, agricultural 
sector, manufacturing sector, services sector, IT sector, in all these areas we 
have reason to be reasonably proud of our achievements compared to other 
developing countries and even compared to certain developed countries. But 
where we have failed, and failed very miserably, I would say, is in the social 
sector and because of that failure in the social sector we have not been able to 
maximise the investments we have made in agriculture, industry, services, etc. 
I am reminded of the advice which Prof. Strumblin gave to Lenin in 1917. 
Lenin had drawn up a blue-print of action, big irrigation schemes, dams, 
heavy industry, etc., and asked for the comments of Prof. Strumblin. He had 
the courage to reply to Lenin saying, "If you don't match the investment you 
have proposed in building dams, heavy machinery industry, improving 
agriculture, etc., with investment in education, all the investment that you 
have proposed in the economic sector will not yield any benefit to the 
people". As early as 1917, he warned the founder of the Communist 
Government in the Soviet Union that investment in education was absolutely 
necessary, if he wanted to maximise the benefits of investment in industry, 
agriculture, services and what not. But, unfortunately, in our country, this 
elementary wisdom has not been translated into practice, in spite of all that we 
had seen as examples from the Soviet Union itself and Western Europe, which 
have progressed considerably. Lenin accepted that advice and tremendous 
improvement was made in their educational system, particularly, in science 
education. That is why their economy could yield to the maximum extent. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, when I speak of the significant omission of 
education in the President's Speech, I would like to invite your attention to 
paragraph 49 of the Address. I think about four pages have been spent on 
Foreign Policy. In fact, it is for the first time in my memory, I find that we 
have been taken round all the countries of the world just to explain to us what 
is being done in our relations with Russia, Iran, Gulf countries, United States, 
Latin America, East Asia and others. While so much importance is being 
given to the Foreign Policy, which runs into four pages, education is given 
only half a page. And what do we read there? There is nothing beyond saying 
that "the nation's commitment to universalisation of elementary education is 
reflected in our move to make free and compulsory education", etc. It says that 
University Grants Commission Act will be amended and the UGC will be 
restructured.    I come to the specific point 
293 

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
about our failure in higher education because the UGC has been mentioned 
here. What is happening today, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, is that the UGC has 
been reduced to a funding agency for the Central Universities. There are 245 
Universities in this country. There are only 17 Central Universities. But, if 
you look into the money that is being spent and the proportion in which the 
money is being spent, you will find that the UGC spends about 62 per cent on 
the non-Plan expenditure of the Central Universities alone. And, another 20 to 
22 per cent on the affiliated colleges of the Delhi University. The result is that 
16 to 17 Central Universities get the bulk of the funds available with the 
University Grants Commission. They have an argument. The Ministry of 
Human Resource Development has an argument that the State Universities 
are the responsibility of the States. Theoretically, yes, the State Universities 
have to be funded by the State Governments. But everyone knows today the 
financial position of the State Governments. To say that they are bankrupt is a 
minor form of presenting the situation in the States today. Even the States 
which are considered to be economically at the top, are not able to meet the 
very basic and elementary demands like paying salaries on the first of the 
month or giving funds for maintaining roads and buildings or paying the 
petrol bills for the Government cars. I am not exaggerating as one who has 
observed things very carefully, I say that the State finances all over India are 
so much in crisis that to expect them to spend money on the universities is to 
expect the impossible for the next few years. Unless the new Finance 
Commission recommends something very radical and throws open new 
avenues of resources for the States or unless the States themselves change 
their conventional methods of budgeting and take bold decisions on certain 
sectors, the States will continue in this sorry plight and who suffers worst, it is 
education. 
If you go to every State and examine the budget, you will find the 
worst sufferer would be the colleges, the secondary schools, the elementary 
schools and then, of course, the universities. There are universities which are 
not able to buy the latest books, which are not able to build up a proper 
library, which are not able to access information through the modern devices 
and they are also not able to keep the buildings properly repaired. There is a 
total ban on filling up vacancies and I am sure this is known to the Members 
of this hon. House. 
No vacancy is allowed to be filled up in most of the universities and 
they are not allowed even to create the staff for new departments. 
294 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Departments are created but there is a total ban on creation of new staff 
saying that some other posts should be surrendered, if you want to start a new 
department with new staff. Without exaggerating in any way, this is the 
position all over India. 
The result is that the Delhi University, which is, I am sorry to use the 
word, pampered compared with some of the best universities in the country, 
in the State from which I am elected like Mumbai University, Pune 
University. They were some of the best universities in the whole country. But 
they are denied funds. And when we represent to the University Grants 
Commission to change their present policy of funding, introduce a new 
policy, they say, "we are bound by our charter". When we find out the charter, 
it permits you to maintain quality education, and quality education cannot be 
introduced or maintained without financial support, then, they throw up their 
hands in helplessness. 
I have myself written to the hon. Minister saying that the whole 
system has to be changed otherwise we will have to write off education in this 
country. We will produce third-rate graduates from second-rate colleges, who 
will find themselves unemployed because they are also unemployable. There 
are a few institutions here and there which are able to manage and they are 
surviving as quality institutions. The point that I am trying to make is, if 
education is not given the importance that it deserves, we would be failing in 
the objective which we have placed before us of lifting India to the level of a 
developed nation in 2020 and that dream may have to be extended further by 
20 years more. 
Equally sad is the state of health care in the country. Under the 
Human Development Index criteria we are placed at 134: Many of the Sub-
Saharan countries of Africa, are much above us in the HDI. We are a country 
which produces satellites which go into the stratosphere. We have constituted 
an Atomic Energy Commission which with the help of other scientists has 
produced atom bombs. We can do anything that other scientists and 
technologists are boasting of doing. But, when it comes to health care, our 
standards are lower than some of the Sub-Saharan countries of Africa. That is 
why I say that we cannot meet the aspirations or fulfil the expectations of the 
people unless we give them proper health care and proper educational 
facilities. 
295 

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
My last point is, no mention has been made in this Address about 
good governance as an objective. This is a problem which is now looming 
large like a small speck. I am saying with full sense of responsibility that in 
many States there is no governance, leave alone good governance. Many 
States, because of various reasons, are plunged into anarchy. Mafia gangs 
have taken over and gang wars and caste wars are going on and the 
administration is just sitting back. In fact, in certain States, particularly in the 
North-East, I am told that the officers are paying tax to the people to make 
sure that their houses are not attacked. Good governance even in well 
administered States, will not qualify for good governance in the correct sense 
of the term. Good governance means, governance of Governments rooted in 
values, rooted in ethics and rooted in principles. If the Government does not 
show an example of being above corruption, or being in control of those who 
are indulging in corruption, how can we talk of good governance? Corruption 
in Government continues unabated in a worst form than ever before. We have 
developed a sort of tolerance to corruption. We have accepted it as inevitable 
in a system like this. Unless the Government shows its determination to fight 
corruption in its own house, we will not be able to tell doctors, educationists, 
businessmen, politicians, etc. that you should not be indulging in  corruption. 
Therefore, I consider this omission about the social sector and about good 
governance and the determination to fight corruption as a significant 
omission. I am not saying that I am not joining the Vote of Thanks. With 
these words of reservation, I join my voice with the Vote of Thanks that is 
proposed for the President for his Address. Thank you.
